title: Gold necklace with coin pendants

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917

altText: A Roman gold necklace with gold coins hanging from it as pendants. Each coin carries a head shown in side view, a portrait of a Roman emperor.

context: A Roman gold necklace of the 3rd century CE that includes coins of the emperor Alexander Severus as pendants. Wearing coins as jewelry shows both their value as gold and the way Romans used coin portraits to spread an emperor's image.

descriptions.k: This necklace is made of gold. Little gold coins hang from it. Each coin has a face on it, seen from the side. Romans wore this a very long time ago. Why would someone wear coins as jewelry?
descriptions.g12: This is a Roman gold necklace with real gold coins hanging from it. Each coin shows the side view of a head, a picture of a Roman emperor. People wore coins as jewelry because they were shiny and valuable. Look at how the coins repeat. What would it feel like to wear this?
descriptions.g35: Romans made this gold necklace around the 3rd century CE and hung gold coins from it. The coins show the emperor Alexander Severus in profile, which means a side view of his head. Coins were small, portable portraits that traveled across the Empire. Look at how the coins hang from the chain. Why might someone turn money into jewelry?
descriptions.g68: This necklace transforms coins into jewelry. The pendants are coins of the emperor Alexander Severus, who ruled in the early 3rd century CE, and each carries a portrait in profile. Roman coins spread the image of the ruler across a huge empire, so a necklace like this combines wealth, fashion, and a link to power. Gold was valuable, and the necklace may also have been a way to store wealth. How does an object change when money becomes ornament?
descriptions.g910: A necklace of gold coins collapses the categories of currency, jewelry, and political image. Coins of Alexander Severus carry his portrait in profile, a standard format that made rulers visible throughout the Empire. Wearing the coins displays wealth, and may also have expressed connection to the emperor, although the record does not tell us the wearer's intention. Consider how the repeated profile heads create rhythm along the necklace and how the same object might have been read as savings, adornment, or loyalty.
descriptions.g1112: This necklace invites several readings at once: as jewelry, as a store of value, and as a collection of imperial portraits circulating on the body. Coins of Alexander Severus, a ruler of the early 3rd century CE, carry stylized profile portraits that served the state's ideology, and the act of wearing them recasts that imagery as personal display. The record does not reveal the wearer's motives or the necklace's original context, so claims about political loyalty or economic strategy remain speculative. Consider how an object can be money, art, and propaganda at once.

teacherNote.context: A Roman gold necklace of the 3rd century CE with coins of the emperor Alexander Severus as pendants. The Met's tags note the profile portrait heads on the coins.
directions: Ask students to design a coin with a symbol that represents their class and explain why they chose it.
Discuss why governments put portraits or symbols on money, and compare with coins students know.
Compare wearing money as jewelry with other ways people show wealth or belonging.
